question: doi-10-1111-jtsa-12843#Q6
text: According to the paper, what change size Δ_μ,m appears in the forecast errors of a perfectly specified AR(1) forecasting model after a change of size δ_μ,m in the mean of the raw data?
reference: Δ_μ,m = δ_μ,m(1 − φ), where φ is the autoregressive parameter.
marking: Required: Δ_μ,m = δ_μ,m(1 − φ), with φ the autoregressive parameter. Also correct: δ_μ,m at the first post-change point, then δ_μ,m(1 − φ) from the next point on; deriving the AR(1) case from the general ARMA formula Δ_μ,m = δ_μ,m(1 − Σφ_j)Σψ_l(θ), with the expansion of 1/θ(z) written either as Σψ_l(θ) z^l or as Σψ_l(θ). Not required: the general ARMA formula.

answers.text: Δ_μ,m = δ_μ,m(1 − φ).

For an AR(1) model, φ₁ = φ and θ = 1, so ψ₀ = 1 and ψₗ = 0 for l ≥ 1. The formula of [location] gives:

Δ_μ,m = δ_μ,m (1 − φ)

So the mean change in the forecast errors is the raw-data mean change scaled by one minus the autoregressive coefficient.

question: doi-10-1007-s00180-023-01377-x#Q15
text: On what does the paper base its view that the AR(1) estimates from GTMSE, MSCE and GPL on the temperature data are realistic?

The authors conclude that the shrinkage is beneficial compared with the model estimated by MSE.
marking: Required: climatologists expect the AR(1) parameter to be positive; the GTMSE, MSCE and GPL estimates are positive and similar to those of earlier climate studies, whereas MSE_h gives a negative estimate. Also correct: adding that the conventional MSE also gives a positive AR(1) estimate (0.558), close to GPL's. Not required: the cited studies by name; the estimates' values.

answers.text:
The [location]: those estimates are positive (0.691, 0.634, 0.532), matching climatologists' expectation of a positive AR(1) parameter for temperature series, and similar to values reported in the climate literature (Hartmann et al. 2013; Cahill et al. 2015; Rahmstorf et al. 2017). By contrast, MSE_h's estimate was −0.786, which the authors read as unrealistic over-shrinkage.

Caveats the paper itself notes: the comparison is qualitative, based on a single series, and MSE₁'s estimate (0.558) is also positive.

The paper bases this on consistency with published estimates in the climate literature — specifically Hartmann et al. (2013), Cahill et al. (2015), and Rahmstorf et al. (2017) — whose AR(1) estimates for global temperature data are similar to those produced by GTMSE, MSCE and GPL (around 0.53–0.69), unlike MSE_h's −0.786.

question: doi-10-1016-j-ejor-2022-04-040#Q11
text: When do common seasonal components (PIC(*,S,S)) help forecast accuracy, and when do they harm it?
reference: They help only when the series share very similar seasonal patterns. In the simulation they do well on data with common seasonal components, with moderate gains over PIC(N,N,N), though no better than common initial seasonal indices with individual components (PIC(*,S,N)). On data with individual seasonal components and initial values (the most flexible DGPs) they are much worse than the correct method in accuracy and do poorly in pinball values. The authors recommend them only for homogeneous series; on the M5 data they were chosen for only one of the 11 groups.
marking: Required: they help only for series with very similar seasonal patterns, and they harm accuracy on data with individual seasonal components (and individual initial values). Also correct: they bring no gain over common initial seasonal indices with individual components (PIC(*,S,N)), even on data with common seasonality; they give moderate gains over PIC(N,N,N) on data with common seasonal components; they do poorly in pinball values on the most flexible data. Not required: that on the M5 data they were chosen for only one of the 11 groups. Wrong (overreach): saying common seasonal components improve accuracy in general.

answers.text:
**When they help:**
- When the data-generating process truly has common seasonality (PIC(*,S,S) DGPs), the restrictive methods perform well — e.g. rMAE ≈ 0.95–0.98 vs benchmark when applied to PIC(LS,S,S) data, with gains growing as group size increases (up to ~35% lower pinball for 50 series).
- Benefits are greatest with **short data histories** and **larger groups**, where pooling compensates for few observations per series.

**When they harm:**
- When the DGP has individual seasonal components (flexible DGPs like PIC(*,N,N)), common seasonal components perform very poorly — rMAE up to **1.7–1.9** and pinball values up to **2.0**, i.e. roughly double the error. The top-right corners of the simulation tables show the worst degradation.
- The harm comes from imposing a shared seasonal pattern on series that genuinely differ, biasing all series in the group toward an "average" seasonality that fits none well.

**Practical guidance from the paper:** apply PIC(*,S,S) only to highly homogeneous series with very similar seasonal shapes; otherwise use PIC(*,S,N) (individual seasonal components with common initials/parameters), which is nearly as good when seasonality is common and far more robust when it is not.

**Help:** When the series truly share a seasonal pattern (data from PIC(*,S,S) variants), PIC(*,S,S) variants are the most accurate — e.g., rMAE ≈ 0.95 vs 1.0 for the correct PIC(N,N,N) on common-seasonality data.

**Harm:** When series have individual seasonal components, forcing a common one is very damaging — rMAE rises to 1.55–1.88 on PIC(N,N,N) data, vs ≈1.0–1.02 for PIC(*,S,N). Hence the recommendation: use common seasonal components only for very similar seasonal patterns.

question: doi-10-1007-s00180-023-01377-x#Q8
text: Do multi-step loss functions shrink the coefficients of a conventional linear regression?
reference: No. A conventional regression has no dynamic elements (its persistence vector is zero), so multi-step loss functions impose no shrinkage on its coefficients; the shrinkage is a univariate, dynamic-model effect.
marking: Required: No: a conventional regression has no dynamic elements, so there is no shrinkage of its coefficients. Also correct: adding that this need not hold for regressions with dynamic (ARMA) errors. Wrong: extending the shrinkage to regression coefficients (overreach).

answers.text:
No — not for a static linear regression. [location] states that multi-step loss functions impose **no parameter shrinkage** on static linear regression models, because the persistence vector \(g = 0\), which implies all multi-step coefficients \(c_j = w'F^{j-1}g = 0\), so there is nothing for the loss to shrink.

Caveat: this zero-shrinkage result applies only to static regressions without dynamic state transitions; it does not transfer to dynamic regression models with AR or MA error structures.

No. The paper states that regression has no dynamic elements — its persistence vector g is zero, so all c_j = 0 and the multi-step variance equals the one-step variance. Hence no shrinkage is imposed on regression coefficients; this shrinkage is a univariate time-series phenomenon.

question: doi-10-1093-imaman-dpad028#Q13
text: Why does the paper say that the Log-Normal distribution should be used with care in ETS(M,*,*) models?
reference: Because of the restriction μ = −σ²/2, the maximum likelihood estimate of the scale comes from an equation with two roots: the derivative of the log-likelihood has two roots, so the likelihood is not convex, which may violate the identification and compactness assumptions and make the estimates inconsistent. The closed-form estimate also exists only when the mean of log²(1 + ϵt) is at most 1; otherwise the scale must be found by numerical optimisation.
marking: Required: the likelihood is not convex (because of the restriction μ = −σ²/2), which may make the estimates inconsistent. Also correct, as equal alternatives for the scale estimate: either that its formula has two roots and exists in closed form only when the mean of log²(1 + ϵt) is at most 1 (otherwise numerical optimisation is needed), or that the scale is given by a corrected formula rather than the quadratic root formula. Not required: the two roots, the ≤ 1 condition, the identification and compactness assumptions. Wrong: omitting the non-convex likelihood.

answers.text: Because its scale estimate has issues: the closed-form MLE only exists if the mean squared log-error is ≤ 1, otherwise numerical optimization is needed. It also gives two roots, and the likelihood is not convex, which can make parameter estimates potentially inconsistent.

Per [location]: under the unit-mean restriction (μ = −σ²/2), the concentrated log-likelihood is **non-convex**, creating potential local optima during numerical optimisation, and the MLE of σ² exists only in some cases — the paper references a corrected formula superseding the erroneous closed-form root printed in the 2023 article.
